title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at [Median age] across counties in [Florida], and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "FL"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B01002_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

my_state <- “FL”
my_variable <- “B01002_001”
county_data <- get_acs( geography = “county”, variables = my_variable, state = my_state, year = 2023, survey = “acs5” )

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 67  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                     variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                    <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 12001 Alachua County, Florida  B01002_001     32.2   0.2
2 12003 Baker County, Florida    B01002_001     38.1   0.7
3 12005 Bay County, Florida      B01002_001     41.4   0.3
4 12007 Bradford County, Florida B01002_001     40.5   1.2
5 12009 Brevard County, Florida  B01002_001     46.8   0.2
6 12011 Broward County, Florida  B01002_001     41.3   0.2


[There are 67 rows which matches the number of counties in Florida.]

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                      estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                        <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Lafayette County, Florida     41.8   2.6    6.22
 2 Liberty County, Florida       39.1   2.1    5.37
 3 Glades County, Florida        45.8   1.9    4.15
 4 Gulf County, Florida          47.3   1.5    3.17
 5 Bradford County, Florida      40.5   1.2    2.96
 6 Holmes County, Florida        42.4   1.2    2.83
 7 Jefferson County, Florida     47     1.3    2.77
 8 Calhoun County, Florida       41.8   0.9    2.15
 9 Hamilton County, Florida      40.6   0.8    1.97
10 Gilchrist County, Florida     42.7   0.8    1.87


[Lafeytte County has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate. It has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate at 6.22%]

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 4 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    59
2 Low confidence      3
3 Moderate            5


[I changed the reliability thresholds to 2% and 4% since the original 5% and 10% thresholds would have placed most counties in the high-confidence category. Of Florida’s 67 counties, 59 have high-confidence estimates, 5 have moderate-confidence estimates, and 3 have low-confidence estimates.]

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                     myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                     <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 12001 Alachua County, Florida    32.2    0.2  281751    NA
2 12003 Baker County, Florida      38.1    0.7   28186    NA
3 12005 Bay County, Florida        41.4    0.3  181368    NA
4 12007 Bradford County, Florida   40.5    1.2   27888    NA
5 12009 Brevard County, Florida    46.8    0.2  620533    NA
6 12011 Broward County, Florida    41.3    0.2 1946127    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 4  ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         59        369666.
2 Low confidence           3          9336.
3 Moderate                 5         18118.


[High-confidence counties have an average population of 369,666. Low-confidence counties have an average population of 9,336. According to this pattern, smaller counties tend to have less reliable estimates of median age.This means policymakers should be careful about making decisions based on the median-age estimates for small counties since there’s more uncertainty in the estimates.]
[We know the least about Lafayette county, Liberty county, and Glades county. Lafayette County has the highest relative margin of error at 6.22%, followed by Liberty County at 5.37%. The higher margin of error means that there is more uncertainty around the median-age estimates for these counties than for most other counties in Florida.Given the pattern displayed in the analysis, these counties have smaller populations and therefore larger margin of errors. The ACS uses a sample of households rather than collecting information from every person.Smaller counties have fewer people and so have smaller samples. With fewer observations, it is harder to produce precise estimates. This further causes a larger margin of error. This can definitely create problems for equitable funding throughout the state.If a state agency used median age to allocate funding it would create problems if they assumed each counties estimate is equally reliable. Major government service like healthcare and senior services can be based off of the age counts in counties.If the estimate for a small county is inaccurate, the county could receive too much or too little funding. This would most likley impact young and older populations who often require greater care. It’s safe to assume smaller counties are vulnerable to having their needs overlooked and so policymakers should consider MOE when using ACS data.]

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Website= folder of .html files plus a computer thats always on Quartos going to write your .html You write .qmd files and then quarto the machine converts to .html Quarto reads the file from top to bottom, finds code chunks, and sends them to R to get results back, then glues text results into html. If theres errors in the code chunks wont be able to change them to html In R studio you can use about .qmd to get the template
Anatomy of .qmd: YAML Code chunks
“(R) library(tidycensus) 2+2 “
Files + Folders: Anything .qmd we can edit (theres a bunch in there about me, weekly notes, assignments, etc. Quarto.yml ar the settings for the whole website _freeze/ → quarto Use Rprject (files like data, docs) so you can know which project space your working in Gitignore → Gil Renivron → R (secrets) Docs → the internet, your finished website - when you press render on your website it creates this and turns it into a .html format Index.html → website rule= ask for a folder, you get the folders index.html Yourname.github.io/ → docs/index.html Weekly notes is inside the docs folder Name yurfirst index after this class
Git/Github/Github Desktop:
Git= version tracker is invisible and runs on the computer Git is constantly tracking changes in r studio, taking notes of everything you do Githu.com= website that stores a copy of your folder, makes your folders and files public Github desktop= buttons that tell git what to do “COMMIT” → “save a labele snapshot” - lives on your computer Commiting and saving are not the same thing, when you click commit on github you can forever see all the changes you made in your code “PUSH” → “send my screenshot to GitHub.com” Makes your changes public For the semester she will give us .qmd, I’ll edit, save, commit, push
R script: Code only Like a sandbox Console good for drafting it won’t save Click on + button at top to get started Can create new quorto document You can tell what project your working in based on the name in the right top hand corner getwd() way of seeing what folder your working in Respository= name of foder, collection of files linked to github MUSA-5080 Portfolio-template is the repository with all the folders inside it
Index.qmd is the render button, your going to edit the about and index and unless you click on inex.qmd it wont create the actual website.
The loop: Edit in RStudio → Save → Render → Commit → Push → wait 2 min → refresh Link to github desktop portfolio: https://github.com/mayalis-upenn/MUSA-5080-portfolio
In files: C:-portfolio


I learned the flow of how projects will be done in this course. Edit in RStudio → Save → Render → Commit → Push → wait 2 min → refresh
